Louisiana property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Louisiana Tax Commission hears real and personal property appeals from board of review actions; hearings begin within ten days of receiving the certified assessment lists. (La. R.S. 47:1989; source)
  • All Louisiana Tax Commission decisions are final unless appealed to district court within thirty days. (La. R.S. 47:1989(D); source)
  • Taxpayer dissatisfied with a final Tax Commission decision may sue within thirty days in the district court for the parish where the Commission is domiciled or where the property is located. (La. R.S. 47:1998; source)
  • A taxpayer who sues must pay taxes under protest (or timely move to set bond/security); undisputed taxes are paid without protest. (La. R.S. 47:1998; source)
  • Board of review hears owners' complaints on assessments; its determinations are final unless appealed to the Tax Commission under Commission rules. (La. R.S. 47:1992 (board of review); source)
  • Board of review must convene hearings on or before September 15 and certify the list to the Tax Commission on or before October 20 each year; assessors certify rolls to the board on or before October 1. (La. R.S. 47:1992 (board of review); source)
  • Land and residential improvements are assessed at 10% of fair market value. (La. Const. art. VII, sec. 18(A); source)
  • Since Acts 2024 No. 774 and Acts 2025 No. 411 (eff. Jan. 1, 2026), Louisiana auctions tax liens rather than the property at first stage; winner gets a recorded tax lien certificate. (La. R.S. 47:2153; source)
  • Auction participants may be required to post a deposit up to $1,000. (La. R.S. 47:2153(C)(5); source)

title: Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

What the official sources say

  • Louisiana inheritance tax law (R.S. 47:2401-2426) was repealed by Act 822 of 2008; no inheritance tax receipts issued after January 1, 2012. (Inheritance and Estate Transfer Taxes | Louisiana Department of Revenue; source)
  • Estate transfer tax (R.S. 47:2431-2437) equals the federal state death tax credit; because that credit is repealed, no state estate transfer tax is due for deaths after December 31, 2004. (Inheritance and Estate Transfer Taxes | Louisiana Department of Revenue; source)
  • R.S. 47:2436 requires an estate transfer tax return where tax is due or the net estate is $60,000 or more. (Inheritance and Estate Transfer Taxes | Louisiana Department of Revenue; source)

Does Louisiana have an estate tax or inheritance tax?

No state death tax is due on a Louisiana estate today. The state repealed its inheritance tax, and its estate transfer tax only ever existed to capture a federal credit that no longer exists.

According to the Louisiana Department of Revenue, Act 822 of the 2008 Regular Session repealed the inheritance tax law in R.S. 47:2401 to 2426, and from January 1, 2012 no receipts are issued for inheritance tax regardless of the date of death. The estate transfer tax in R.S. 47:2431 to 2437 equals the federal credit for state death taxes. Because that credit was replaced by a deduction for deaths after December 31, 2004, the department says no state estate transfer tax is due for those deaths.

For heirs of a Louisiana house, that means the sale proceeds are not reduced by a state death tax. The money questions that remain are federal, plus the cost and time of moving title.

What does Louisiana law still ask heirs to file?

One filing rule stays on the books: an estate transfer tax return is required where tax is due or where the deceased's net estate is $60,000 or more. R.S. 47:2436 says the heirs or legatees file it, and that it is mailed to the collector of revenue and to the person designated as tax collector under R.S. 47:2417.

The statute sets the timing at nine months after death, or before a United States estate tax return is filed, whichever comes first. It also requires the return to list the full name of the deceased, residence at death, estate value, whether a federal return was filed, safety deposit box contents omitted from the estate and any omitted assets, with an explanation.

The Revenue Department's page was last updated on February 20, 2025. Whether a return is still expected on an estate with no tax due is a question for the succession attorney or a CPA, since the page and statute both keep the $60,000 trigger in place.

How much of an estate does the federal government tax in 2026?

Only large estates owe federal estate tax: the basic exclusion amount for people who die in 2026 is $15,000,000. The IRS states that the Working Families Tax Cuts law, signed July 4, 2025, raised the basic exclusion amount to that level.

The same IRS page lists the annual gift exclusion for 2026 as $19,000 per donee. Estates under the exclusion amount owe no federal estate tax, and the filing threshold for year-of-death 2026 is also $15,000,000.

ItemAmount or ruleSource
Louisiana inheritance taxRepealed, no receipts since Jan. 1, 2012Louisiana Department of Revenue
Louisiana estate transfer taxNone due for deaths after Dec. 31, 2004Louisiana Department of Revenue
Estate transfer tax returnRequired if net estate is $60,000 or more (R.S. 47:2436)Louisiana Legislature
Federal basic exclusion, 2026 death$15,000,000IRS
Federal annual gift exclusion, 2026$19,000 per doneeIRS

Will an heir who sells an inherited Louisiana house owe income tax?

An heir's gain is usually figured from the home's value on the date of death, not from what the deceased paid. The IRS explains that the basis of inherited property is generally the fair market value on the decedent's date of death, whether or not the executor files a federal estate tax return.

That is why a house inherited and sold soon afterward often produces little or no taxable gain. The gain, if any, is the sale price less that stepped basis and allowed selling costs. Two cases deserve a closer look:

  • Community property: IRS Publication 551 says that when either spouse dies, the total value of community property, even the part belonging to the survivor, generally becomes the basis of the entire property.
  • Special valuation: for some farm or business property and for property whose value is set under estate tax rules, the basis can follow that valuation instead.

Keep the date-of-death appraisal. Pub. 551 notes that if no Schedule A reports the estate tax value, the appraised value at death used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes can establish basis, so a written valuation helps in any case.

How does an heir get legal title to sell a Louisiana house?

A house cannot be sold by heirs just because the owner died; title has to be moved to them through a succession. Louisiana does this through a court proceeding that ends in a judgment of possession, or through a sworn affidavit when the estate qualifies as a small succession.

Code of Civil Procedure art. 3062 says a judgment of possession in a succession is prima facie evidence of the relationship of the parties recognized in it, as heir, legatee, surviving spouse in community or usufructuary, and of their right to possess the estate. A title company will look for that judgment or the equivalent paperwork before it insures a sale.

Louisiana's approach to a surviving spouse also differs from most states. Civil Code art. 890 gives the surviving spouse a usufruct over the decedent's share of the community property, to the extent the decedent has not disposed of it by will, when descendants survive. The usufruct ends when the surviving spouse dies or remarries. A usufruct is an interest in the house, so it must be addressed in the paperwork before a sale.

When can a Louisiana family skip court with a small succession affidavit?

Some estates do not need to be opened judicially. Code of Civil Procedure art. 3431 lists three situations:

  • A person domiciled in Louisiana who died intestate.
  • A person domiciled in Louisiana who died testate leaving no immovable property in Louisiana, if the surviving spouse and all persons who would inherit, with or without the testament, agree to waive probate.
  • A person domiciled outside Louisiana who died intestate or whose testament was probated by court order of another state.

Under art. 3432, at least two persons, including the surviving spouse if there is one and at least one heir, sign a sworn affidavit. With no surviving spouse, at least two heirs sign, and if there is only one heir a second person with actual knowledge signs too. The affidavit sets out the date of death and domicile, marital status, heirs and their relationships, a description of the property sufficient to identify immovable property for transfer, the value of each item and the total, and each heir's interest.

An heir who does not sign must either be unlocatable after reasonable diligence or have received thirty days' written notice by U.S. mail and not objected. Signing the affidavit also accepts the succession for an heir, so families should understand the debts of the estate first.

What happens to the property tax, mortgage and utilities while an estate is open?

Those bills keep running whether or not a succession has been opened. The estate tax rules above say nothing about carrying costs, so the heirs generally cover them or the sale proceeds do.

Practical points for a Louisiana family handling a vacant house:

  • Keep insurance active, and ask the carrier how a vacant house is treated.
  • Notify the lender and the parish assessor's office of the death if mail is going to the old address.
  • Photograph the condition of the house and keep copies of repair bills in case an executor or other heir questions the sale price.

Where heirs disagree, a cash offer does not settle the dispute, but a signed judgment or affidavit does give all of them one version of who owns what.

How does a cash sale work when the house is in an open Louisiana estate?

A cash buyer can close once title is in the hands of the people who are entitled to sell, so the first step is the same as for any buyer: prove authority. Expect to provide the judgment of possession or the filed affidavit, a copy of any will, and payoff information on liens.

Many heirs live out of state and cannot clear out a house, cut the grass or fix storm damage from a distance. Selling as-is spares them those chores. The estate and tax numbers above matter most for deciding what to do with the proceeds, so a call with an estate attorney or CPA before closing is time well spent. Our team does not give legal or tax advice; this guide only collects what the official sources say.

More questions about Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Louisiana charge an inheritance tax?

No. The Louisiana Department of Revenue says Act 822 of 2008 repealed the inheritance tax, and no inheritance tax receipts are issued since January 1, 2012, regardless of date of death.

Does Louisiana have a state estate tax in 2026?

No state estate transfer tax is due for deaths after December 31, 2004, according to the Department of Revenue, because the federal credit it relied on was replaced by a deduction.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for a death in 2026?

$15,000,000. The IRS states the basic exclusion amount for 2026 is $15,000,000 under the law signed July 4, 2025.

Is the sale of an inherited house in Louisiana taxable?

Only the gain above the stepped-up basis is taxable. The IRS says inherited property generally takes the fair market value on the date of death as its basis, so little gain is common when the sale follows soon after.

Do I need a court case to sell my parent's house in Louisiana?

Not always. A small succession affidavit can be used when art. 3431 allows it, such as an intestate Louisiana domiciliary. Estates with a will covering Louisiana land generally need a judicial succession.

Who gets the house when a Louisiana spouse dies?

It depends on the will and the heirs. If descendants survive, the surviving spouse has a usufruct over the decedent's share of community property under Civil Code art. 890, until death or remarriage, unless the decedent disposed of it by will.

content:
Louisiana Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Lessor must give written notice to vacate allowing at least five days from delivery; for definite-term leases notice may be given up to 30 days before term ends. (La. C.C.P. art. 4701; source)
  • A lessee may waive the notice in a written lease clause. (La. C.C.P. art. 4701; source)
  • Transfer of the leased thing by the lessor does not terminate the lease; tenant may sue lessor for loss from the transfer. (La. C.C. art. 2711; source)
  • Buyer of property subject to a recorded lease takes subject to its provisions if the lease was recorded before the buyer's document. (La. R.S. 9:2721(B); source)

How does an eviction work in Louisiana, step by step?

A Louisiana eviction is a fast, summary court case that begins only after a written notice to vacate has gone unanswered. The steps below follow the Code of Civil Procedure, title XI, which governs the eviction of tenants and occupants.

  1. The lessor or owner delivers a written notice to vacate (art. 4701 or 4702).
  2. If the tenant or occupant does not comply, the owner has the court cite them to appear by a rule to show cause why possession should not be delivered (art. 4731). The rule states the grounds.
  3. The court makes the rule returnable no earlier than the third day after service, tries it and hears any defense (art. 4732(A)).
  4. If the owner wins, or the tenant fails to answer or appear, the court renders a judgment of eviction immediately (art. 4732(B)).
  5. If the tenant has not complied within twenty-four hours, the court issues a warrant to its sheriff, constable or marshal to deliver possession to the owner (art. 4733).

Our companion guide on the eviction notice covers step one in detail. This page picks up at the courthouse.

Which Louisiana court hears an eviction?

A justice of the peace court can hear a residential eviction, and so can the parish or district court. Code of Civil Procedure art. 4912 gives justice of the peace courts jurisdiction, concurrent with the parish or district court, over suits by landowners or lessors to evict occupants or tenants of leased residential premises, regardless of the amount of monthly or yearly rent.

The article also covers some commercial and farm leases. A justice of the peace court may hear evictions of tenants of leased commercial premises and farmland where monthly rent does not exceed $5,000, again regardless of the rent due or the rent for the rest of the lease.

Which courthouse an owner uses depends on where the house sits. For houses in a parish with city courts, parish courts or justice of the peace wards, the clerk of court can say where eviction rules are filed.

How long does each stage of a Louisiana eviction take?

The statute fixes short minimum windows, and real calendars depend on the court. The table gathers the statutory numbers.

StageStatutory timeArticle
Notice to vacateAt least 5 days from deliveryC.C.P. 4701
Hearing on the ruleNot earlier than the third day after serviceC.C.P. 4732(A)
Judgment of eviction effectiveFor not less than 90 daysC.C.P. 4732(B)
Voluntary complianceWithin 24 hours of the judgmentC.C.P. 4733
Suspensive appeal request and bondWithin 24 hours of the judgmentC.C.P. 4735

Adding the minimums, the fastest lawful path takes more than a week from notice delivery, and that assumes the owner files promptly and the court has a hearing slot. We did not find an official average length for Louisiana evictions, so we do not quote one.

What happens at the hearing?

The judge tries the rule on the day it is returnable and hears any defense the tenant raises. The owner should arrive with the lease if there is one, the written notice and proof of when it was delivered, and a record of what is owed.

A tenant who does not answer or appear loses by default: art. 4732(B) says the court shall render a judgment of eviction immediately if the owner is entitled to relief or the lessee or occupant fails to answer or appear. The resulting judgment is effective for not less than ninety days, which gives the owner a window to carry out the order rather than a single day.

Owners who are family members, heirs or buyers should bring documents that show they now hold the lessor's position. Art. 4704 defines lessor to include an assignee or transferee, so title paperwork matters.

Can a tenant appeal an eviction judgment in Louisiana?

Yes, but an appeal does not stop the eviction by itself. Under art. 4735, execution of the judgment is suspended only if the defendant answered the rule under oath pleading an affirmative defense that would entitle them to keep possession, applied for the appeal and filed the appeal bond within twenty-four hours after the judgment.

The amount of the suspensive appeal bond is set by the court, in an amount sufficient to protect the appellee against damage from the appeal. For the owner, the practical effect is that the twenty-four hour window usually decides whether the warrant for possession can issue.

What can a landlord not do while an eviction is in progress?

An owner who skips the court process risks a penalty. Art. 4731(C)(2) says that a lessor's failure to follow that article lets a residential lessee recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, and the tenant may seek a restraining order or injunction. The court may award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party.

After a federally declared disaster, the same article adds a thirty day protection for residents of the declared parishes: a household that has left the home is not treated as having abandoned it during that time. For Louisiana sellers whose rental was hit by a hurricane or flood, that matters when deciding whether the house can be treated as vacant.

Does selling a rented house in Louisiana end the lease?

No. Civil Code art. 2711 provides that the transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease unless the lessor and lessee agreed otherwise. The buyer steps into the picture with the tenant already in the house.

Whether the buyer is bound by the lease depends on recording. Under art. 2712, a third person who acquires an immovable subject to an unrecorded lease is not bound by it, and the lessee, absent a contrary clause in the lease, has an action against the lessor for losses caused by the transfer. R.S. 9:2721 goes the other way for recorded leases: a buyer of property subject to a recorded lease that is not divested by the acquisition takes the property subject to all of its provisions. The statute says this includes any provision for paying a commission to a leasing agent.

A seller should therefore find out before listing whether the lease was ever recorded in the parish conveyance records, and what it says about rent, term and early termination.

What happens to the tenant's security deposit when a Louisiana landlord sells?

The deposit moves with the property. R.S. 9:3251(B) says that when the lessor's interest is transferred during the lease, the transferor must also transfer the deposit to the successor, and the transferor is then relieved of further liability for it. The transferee becomes responsible for returning it when the lease ends.

The general deposit rule in subsection (A) requires return to a residential tenant within one month after the lease ends. The landlord may keep what is reasonably needed to remedy a default or unreasonable wear, and if any is retained, an itemized statement with reasons is due within that month. The tenant must give a forwarding address, and the one-month rule does not apply where the tenant abandons the premises.

Sellers should write the deposit amount into the sale paperwork so it is credited correctly at closing.

Should a Louisiana owner finish the eviction before selling?

It depends on the lease, the case and the owner's patience. Finishing the eviction clears the house for showings, but it takes court time and may mean cleanup of what the tenant leaves behind.

Owners weighing the choice usually compare:

  • Cost and time of finishing a case, including repairs after the tenant leaves.
  • Whether the lease is recorded and would bind a buyer under R.S. 9:2721.
  • Whether the tenant is paying and wants to stay, which changes the picture entirely.
  • A sale as-is with the tenant in place, which transfers the lease and the deposit to the buyer under the statutes above.

Our team also looks at houses that come with tenants or a difficult rental history. The statutes above describe the rules; a Louisiana attorney can advise on a specific lease.

More questions about Louisiana Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Louisiana eviction take after the notice period?

The court may set the hearing no earlier than the third day after service of the rule. If the owner wins, the tenant has twenty-four hours to comply before a warrant issues. Actual timing depends on the court's calendar.

Which court handles evictions in Louisiana?

Justice of the peace courts have concurrent jurisdiction with parish or district courts over residential evictions under art. 4912, whatever the rent. The parish or district court can also hear them.

How long is a Louisiana judgment of eviction good for?

At least ninety days, under art. 4732(B). This gives the owner time to obtain a warrant and have possession delivered.

Does an appeal stop a Louisiana eviction?

Only in narrow cases. The tenant must have answered under oath pleading an affirmative defense, and must apply for the appeal and file the bond within twenty-four hours of the judgment.

Does the lease end if I sell my rented Louisiana house?

No. Civil Code art. 2711 says transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease unless the parties agreed otherwise. A recorded lease binds the buyer under R.S. 9:2721, while an unrecorded lease does not bind a third-party buyer under art. 2712.

What happens to my tenant's deposit if I sell the house?

You must transfer it to the buyer, and you are then relieved of further liability. The buyer must return it at the end of the lease within the time R.S. 9:3251(A) requires.
